cards.front: Recall a key point about Education Policy
cards.back: 1944 Education Act: introduced the tripartite system - grammar schools (academic, 20% via 11+ exam), secondary moderns (practical/vocational, 75%), technical schools (few existed). Supposedly meritocratic but reproduced class inequality - middle-class children disproportionately passed the 11+.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Education Policy
cards.back: 1965: comprehensive education replaced the tripartite system. All pupils attend the same type of school regardless of ability. Aimed to reduce inequality and create social mixing. Evaluation: reduced the stigma of failing the 11+ but streaming within comprehensives reproduced inequality. Some areas retained grammar schools (the grammar school debate continues).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Education Policy
cards.back: 1988 Education Reform Act (Marketisation): introduced the National Curriculum, league tables, Ofsted inspections, and open enrollment (parents choose schools). Schools compete for pupils (like businesses). Smith and Noble: marketisation benefits middle-class parents who can work the system (house prices near good schools, knowledge of admissions). Whitty: creates a 'parentocracy' where educated, affluent parents have most choice.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Education Policy
cards.back: Academies and free schools (2010 onwards): academies are state-funded but independent of local authority control; free schools are set up by parents, teachers or charities. Intended to raise standards through autonomy and innovation. Evaluation: some academies have improved results, but overall evidence is mixed. Critics argue they reduce democratic accountability and increase social segregation.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Education Policy
cards.back: Recent policies: tuition fees for university (policies create a class divide in higher education), pupil premium (additional funding for disadvantaged students - evaluation: helps but is insufficient), and policies to promote social mobility (evaluation: limited success because they don't address structural inequality).

cards.front: What should you know about sociology exam tips?
cards.back: When evaluating education policy, always: describe the policy clearly, explain its intended purpose, evaluate its actual impact on inequality (especially class, gender and ethnicity), and consider unintended consequences.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Marketisation has improved education for everyone by making schools compete and raising standards.
